acts.title: The first commit
acts.sub: Scaffold the repo the same way a cautious human does — one clean chore commit.

acts.title: Three changes, three commits
acts.sub: Split a messy work session into small, reviewable, atomic commits.

acts.title: Ship it calmly
acts.sub: Put the experiment on a branch, then land it without drama — even when a conflict tries to ambush the merge.

steps.title: A blank directory, full of promise
steps.body: You're starting a tiny website from scratch. The first real git act is to give it a repo — git won't do anything useful until it has one.

visual.caption: git init makes the .git directory — objects, refs and the index live inside it.

steps.title: Decide what does NOT belong
steps.body: Before the first commit, add a .gitignore. Node_modules, build output, and that stray debug.log should never be tracked. Deciding what stays out is part of the discipline.

visual.caption: Only the ignore rule is staged so far — still nothing committed.

steps.title: Stage the scaffold, then stop
steps.body: Now stage the three files that make up the project shell: package.json, the lockfile and the README. Notice the craft: you only stage what belongs to THIS commit, not 'everything that exists'.

steps.title: The first commit
steps.body: Commit the shell as a single logical unit. The prefix chore marks housekeeping — no user-visible behavior yet. And the subject is short: 26 characters, well under the 50 limit.

steps.title: The 50 / 72 rule
steps.body: A human-readable commit is a gift to your future self. Keep the subject under 50 characters — it reads in listings. Wrap detail lines at 72. If the message needs a paragraph, it deserves its own commit.
steps.cmd: git commit -m "fix: reset focus ring" -m "Pressing space no longer keeps the focus ring stuck after the button closes."

steps.title: The trap: six files, one commit
steps.body: A real work session leaves the tree messy. Here: a bug fix, a small feature, some styling, and a stray debug.log, all edited at once. The lazy commit — git add -A; git commit -m "update" — buries everything under one blob.

visual.caption: git status shows 6 changes at once — this is the exactly the situation a careful human splits apart.

steps.title: Group by logical change
steps.body: Sort the files the way a reviewer thinks: the bug fix alone, the feature's two files together, the styling alone — and the debug.log ignored, never committed. Three logical changes, three commits. No reason to rush.

steps.title: Commit the fix — small and atomic
steps.body: One fix, one commit, a prefix that says fix, a subject that says WHAT and not HOW. Reviewers can read this line and instantly decide it's safe. That's the whole point of atomic commits.
steps.cmd: git commit -m "fix: reset focus ring on space bar"

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

steps.title: The feature lands next
steps.body: The feature spans two files, so stage them together: nav.tsx and nav.css are ONE change — a sidebar isn't complete without its styles. Then commit it with the feat prefix.
steps.cmd: git add src/nav.tsx src/nav.css && git commit -m "feat: add sticky mobile sidebar"

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

steps.title: Style is its own chore
steps.body: Visual-only tweaks get the style prefix — they change behavior of nothing, and the prefix tells everyone so at a glance. Three commits in: chore, fix, feat — each one reviewable in seconds.
steps.cmd: git add src/theme.css && git commit -m "style: align page title spacing"

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

steps.title: Read it like a changelog
steps.body: git log --oneline --graph turns history into a story: chore -> fix -> feat -> style. Each commit is small enough to reason about, and each prefix is a filter. Compare that to one giant 'update stuff' blob — there's no contest.

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

spec.caption: A linear history that reads like a changelog — the reward for atomic commits.

steps.title: Experiment on a branch
steps.body: Next feature is riskier, so it lives on its own branch. git switch -c both creates and jumps to feat/avatar. main stays clean and shippable while you experiment.

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

steps.title: Work happens on the branch
steps.body: The commit lands on feat/avatar, and main doesn't move at all. Risky work beats up the branch, not the trunk. Same atomic discipline: one feature, one commit.

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

steps.title: Jump back to the safe line
steps.body: git switch main moves HEAD back to the main line. Everything you made is still safe on the branch — but the working tree now reflects the shippable trunk. The graph starts to fork.

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

steps.title: The merge comes home, and collides
steps.body: feat/avatar rewrote the avatar header — and main's sidebar refactor touched that exact file too. Same hunk, two truths: Git can't stitch it, so it prints both with <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers and PAUSES. Nobody lost anything yet. Panic button still works: git merge --abort.

visual.caption: The merge pauses, politely, and hands you the decision

steps.title: Pick the truth, tell Git, and continue
steps.body: You want the feature's avatar logic AND main's new sidebar styling — so you keep both hunks, delete the markers, save. git add marks the file resolved, and git merge --continue writes one clean, two-parent merge commit. The day still ships, and nobody panicked.

visual.caption: Markers gone, merge continued, calendar unharmed

steps.title: The whole day, one clean story
steps.body: git log --oneline --graph shows the day's work the way a human actually did it: a chore scaffold, three atomic changes, one forked experiment, one explicit merge. Small commits. Clear prefixes. No 50-file blobs. This is what professionals do.

nodes.msg: fix: reset focus ring on space bar

spec.caption: Six commits, each one logical, one merge, zero panic — a realistic, human day of git.
